assessment:
One tutor. Vampiric Tutor is the only card in the 99 that searches your library for a spell — enumerated over all 96 entries, where the only other cards carrying 'search your library' are Bloodstained Mire and Marsh Flats, and a fetchland's search is a mana question, not a wish. deck-audit reads the axis at 1 copy.

It costs {B} at instant speed, takes any card, puts it on TOP, and bills you two life and your next draw. The top-of-library part sets the timing: cast it at an end step before your untap, so the card you bought is the card you draw. Cast it three turns early and you have spent a card arranging a draw. Pay the two life without thinking about it — Sanctum Seeker, Cruel Celebrant and the lifelink bodies hand it back. It also reveals nothing, which is worth more here than in most decks: there is no counterspell in the 99 and no way to fight over a stack, so the only protection this wish has is that nobody sees it.

Where it points changed with v1.0.1. The twelve bloodline swaps deleted the go-wide kill — 400 Forge games, composite 31/400 against the champion's 50/400 at an interval excluding zero, and combat damage to players falling 29.07 to 18.20 because 1/1 tokens do not connect — and every card that turned a token entry into damage left with it. What is left is a machine that makes bodies and then eats them, plus two checker-passed kill routes that each rest on ONE card: Bloodletter of Aclazotz (stack 003) and Bloodthirsty Conqueror (stacks 004 and 006).

So the wish has one honest job and it is a narrow one. Most of this deck is deep enough not to need it: a castable Vampire is drawn in 95.1% of games at mean turn 2.186, a draw engine in 84.1%, a lord or anthem in 80.2%, a free sacrifice outlet in 77.6% (◆ goldfish, 10,000 seeded games). Never spend the wish on a component that deep. Three things are thin. The death drain is two cards at 37.2%. The Bloodletter pairing assembles in 4.2% of games and 9.6% with the wish spent on it. The Conqueror loop is 7.6% and 14.6%. That gap is the whole of what this card is worth to the deck, and it is measured against exactly one tutor because there is only one.

One thing to decide before you point it at the loop rather than at the board. The pilot's own log entry for 2026-09-01 records losing to a tutored two-card infinite and says plainly that it is tutorability plus two-card infinites, not power level, that turns a pod game salty. Aiming this deck's only search at Bloodthirsty Conqueror is the same move from the other chair. It is a table call, not a maths one, and the maths does not settle it.

tutors.notes: {B}, instant speed, any card, on top, two life and your next draw. Four rules of thumb follow from that shape. Cast it at an end step immediately before your own untap, so the delay costs nothing and the table's mana is already spent. Only cast it when you will cast the card the turn it arrives — a card sitting on top is a card in removal range with a turn's warning. Never buy a component the deck already finds: the four rates above 77% are not what this card is for. And read the mana before the wish, not after: black is 32 sources against a 36 target and the two costs most worth fetching are {1}{B}{B}{B} and {3}{B}{B}. Herald's Horn changes the timing when it is out with Vampire named — the upkeep look puts a Vampire creature card straight into your hand and leaves your draw step intact, so a Vampire fetched the turn before arrives a turn early.

targets.scenario: Opponent 3's end step, turn six. Vito, Thorn of the Dusk Rose has been on the battlefield since turn four and nothing has answered him. You have six lands, one black source untapped for the tutor, and {3}{B}{B} payable on your own turn. Nobody has held up mana since turn four.
targets.why:
This is the fetch that ends the game rather than improving the board, and it is checker-passed. Stack 004 resolves Conqueror beside Vito as a deterministic, shortcut-legal table kill at zero additional mana, and it survives an opponent dying mid-iteration. Stack 006 proves the same loop with Sanguine Bond in Vito's place, word for word. Both pairings share one body, which is why Conqueror is the half to fetch: Vito and Sanguine Bond are interchangeable and Conqueror is not. The rate is what makes the wish worth spending — the pairing assembles in 7.6% of games unassisted and 14.6% with the wish, 3.0% by turn six against 6.3% (◆ goldfish, 10,000 seeded games). Carry the ticket; do not steer the whole game toward it.

Three prices, all real. He lands the turn AFTER the search, so this is a two-turn commitment announced by a card you did not reveal. He is a 5/5 creature, so every iteration's priority window admits instant-speed creature removal — stack 004 names that cost in its own resolution. And {3}{B}{B} on six lands is a cast that leaves you nothing, in a deck with no counterspell and 32 black sources against a 36 target.

The assumption behind 'nobody has held up mana since turn four': I am reading three untapped-and-unspent turns as a table with no instant-speed answer up. That is a model of the table, not a fact about it.

targets.scenario: Opponent 1's end step, turn six. Sanctum Seeker and six other Vampires are on your battlefield and all seven can attack next turn. Opponent 2 is at 14, opponent 3 at 21. You have {1}{B}{B}{B} available on your turn and one black source untapped now.
targets.why:
Stack 003 is checker-passed on exactly this arithmetic. Seven attacking Vampires give seven Sanctum Seeker triggers; Bloodletter doubles each opponent's loss independently because it is your turn, so each seat loses 14, and the seat at 14 is eliminated by state-based actions BEFORE blockers are declared. Your own lifegain is not doubled — Bloodletter replaces only opponents' loss.

Count the attackers, then count them again without Bloodletter. He has flying and no haste, so he does not attack the turn he lands; stack 003's seven attackers include him on a later turn. Six attackers is six triggers and 12 per seat, and a seat at 14 lives on 2. The scenario above is written with seven bodies that can already attack for that reason.

Read the mana before the wish. {1}{B}{B}{B} is the only cost in the 99 with three or more identical coloured pips — enumerated over every mana cost in cards.json — and black is the deck's shortest colour at 32 sources against a 36 target (deck-audit, Karsten 90%). Master of Dark Rites is the exception worth knowing: tap and sacrifice another creature for {B}{B}{B}, spendable on Vampire, Cleric and Demon spells, and Bloodletter is a Vampire Demon. With the Master already down and a token to eat, the cast is a turn earlier than the lands say — but deck-facts flags the limit, that mana pays for SPELLS and an activated ability is not a spell.

The pairing assembles in 4.2% of games and 9.6% with the wish, 1.5% by turn six against 4.0% (◆ goldfish, 10,000 seeded games).

citations.quote: Your cards should do something to all three seats or win the game

targets.scenario: Turn five. Viscera Seer is on the battlefield with four eminence tokens beside it, no drain has been drawn, and all three opponents are above 30. Opponent 2 has held four open for two turns and has cast nothing.
targets.why:
You have the outlet and no bill. The deck holds exactly two cards that turn a death into life loss — Blood Artist and Cruel Celebrant — and the pair is drawn in 37.2% of games, 24.7% by turn six, mean turn 4.35 (◆ goldfish, 10,000 seeded games). That is the thinnest component in the deck apart from the two one-card kill routes, and it is a component the wish can actually replace, unlike the four sitting above 77%.

Take Celebrant over Blood Artist when the whole table matters, and the difference is in the oracle text rather than in a rating: Blood Artist drains one TARGET PLAYER per death, Celebrant drains EACH OPPONENT. Three-to-one in a pod. With Celebrant down, sacrificing a token bills every seat without an attack connecting, which is the half of the plan the 400-game Forge result said the deck could not get from combat.

State the read: four open mana in a seat that has cast nothing for two turns is a sweeper in my model, not a fact on the board. If it is a sweeper, Celebrant is the card that makes it pay you — every creature you lose drains each opponent for one and gains you one, and Edgar rebuilds from the command zone. If it is a counterspell, this wish was cast at an end step and reveals nothing, so it is a spell they can answer and not a plan they can see.

The limit on this fetch: engine.json's conversion-to-output arrow carries no verified_by, and no artifact measures an outlet and a drain together. The two rates above are for cards being drawn, side by side.

citations.quote: buy resilience instead of restraint where you can

targets.scenario: Opponent 1's end step, turn seven. You have nine bodies, Anointed Procession and Mondrak, Glory Dominus on the battlefield, and lethal on the next swing. Opponent 3 has drawn heavily, is on eight untapped lands and has cast nothing since turn four.
targets.why:
Fetch the card that keeps the board rather than the card that grows it. Teferi's Protection is the only card in the 99 whose text phases your permanents out and stops your life total changing — enumerated over all 96 entries, and no other card carries 'phase out', 'protection from everything' or 'life total can't change'. It matters because the other four protection cards are narrower than this board needs: Flawless Maneuver and Akroma's Will name creatures only, so the two doublers are uncovered; Boros Charm's indestructible mode does reach them but answers neither an exile wipe nor a drain; Deflecting Swat redirects one spell or ability. deck-audit reads sweepers at 0 copies, so after a wipe resolves this deck has no reply at all.

Say the read: eight untapped lands and three quiet turns is a stocked hand in my model. That is the assumption the fetch is priced on, and it is the one the deck can least afford to be wrong about with nine bodies committed.

The delay is the reason for the end-step timing. The card goes on TOP, so you draw it on your turn and it is live from then on; a wipe cast before your draw step is one this wish did not buy an answer to. Once it is in hand it also covers the other thing that has beaten this deck: on 2026-09-01 an opponent's tutored two-card infinite closed before lethal resolved. Teferi's Protection does not stop them winning — it stops your life total changing until your next turn, which against a drain kill is the difference between losing and getting your swing.

citations.quote: prefer committing at the end step before your own turn so the table's chances to respond are spent

gaps: Forerunner of the Legion is gone from this guide and it was not a stale card — it was a misclassification. Its trigger reveals a Vampire from your library and puts it on top; it does not search, so `deck_tutors` never counted it and the guide should not have. It is also no longer in the 99. Nothing about the deck's Vampire-only search constraint survives here, because there is no Vampire-only search.

The goldfish models a cast tutor as a wildcard that fills ONE missing any_of group, pays its mana and costs a turn when it puts the card on top. It does not model the two life, the lost draw, or the choice between two missing groups. Because this deck has exactly one tutor, every *_assisted figure quoted here is Vampiric Tutor and nothing else — which makes the assisted-minus-unassisted gap an unusually clean measure of this one card, and still a ceiling on it.

Nothing measures fetch-versus-hold. No artifact prices the two life, the turn of delay, or the value of revealing nothing against a table's interaction, so every timing call in this guide is coaching judgment sitting on top of measured assembly rates. The one logged game that bears on it is one game.

strategic_frame.json is STALE against v1.0.1 and this guide does not follow it. Its archetype names Purphoros, Impact Tremors, Warleader's Call, Corpse Knight and Witty Roastmaster as the deck's converters, and Ocelot Pride, Shared Animosity and Pact of the Serpent among its engines; none of those eight is in the current 99. The grounding used here is engine.json (rebuilt 2026-09-02 against decklist_sha256 7ce22fd6) and goldfish_metrics.json, which carry the same sha as decklist.txt. Reported, not edited.

Six of the eleven checker-passed stacks resolve boards holding cards the bloodline merge removed — 001 and 005 (Exquisite Blood), 007 (Throne of the God-Pharaoh), 008 and 009 (Purphoros, Impact Tremors, Warleader's Call) and 011 (Mirkwood Bats). This guide cites only 003, 004 and 006, whose boards sit entirely inside the current 99. The other proofs are still true about those cards; they are no longer true about this deck.

There is no graveyard answer in the 99 to fetch. Reading every entry, the only cards naming a graveyard are Takenuma, Abandoned Mire (your own), Nighthawk Scavenger (a count of card types), Immersturm Predator (exile up to one card on tap) and The Haunt of Hightower (a counter). Against a reanimator seat this tutor buys speed and never an answer, and a tutor cannot buy a class the deck does not hold.
